name: Lævateinn
maker: Unnamed (forged with rune magic in some readings)
powers: The only weapon said able to slay the rooster Viðófnir at the top of the world tree.
description: Lævateinn, the 'wounding wand', is the blade of the poem Fjölsvinnsmál, the only weapon said to be able to slay the rooster Viðófnir that perches at the top of the world tree. The wand lies in a chest beside the giantess Sinmara, bound by nine locks that can be opened only by a feather plucked from Viðófnir's own tail, a riddle-like condition that keeps the weapon out of reach. Scholars debate whether the name means 'wounding-wand' and whether the blade is to be identified with Loki's sword, since the name in the manuscripts may be a late emendation of 'Hævateinn', the 'high-wand'. The weapon's place in the late, riddling poem Fjölsvinnsmál sets it apart from the better-known Eddic swords. Lævateinn is nonetheless a favourite of catalogue-writers and of modern fantasy that draws on Old Norse weaponry.
source: Poetic Edda (Fjölsvinnsmál)

name: Lasabrjótur
powers: Said to open locks, fetters, and binding magic.
description: Lasabrjótur, the lock-breaker of the Huld manuscript, a stave said to open locks, fetters, and bonds. Its name literally means 'breaker of latches'. It was the kind of sign that made the Icelandic staves feared as well as respected, promising a power over iron and bindings that no ordinary key could match. In the collection of Geir Vigfússon, compiled at Akureyri in 1860, the stave is recorded with the simple instruction that it serves 'to open a lock without a key' — a task that in folk practice extended to releasing fetters, opening chests, and loosening binding magic laid on people or property. Users were cautioned to draw the sign with care, since a stave aimed at another's lock was itself a threat.
source: Huld manuscript (Lbs 4626 8vo, 1860)

name: Lukkustafir
powers: A set of ten signs each drawn for good fortune in a different undertaking.
description: Lukkustafir, the luck staves of the Huld manuscript, a set of ten separate signs each drawn for good fortune in a different undertaking. The grimoire gives them as a family of practical charms for games, trade, travel, and daily life, so that the luck seeker could choose the sign that matched the task. They remain among the most reproduced of the Icelandic staves, second only to Vegvísir and Ægishjálmr in modern popularity. Unlike the aggressive defensive staves, the luck signs were turned to peaceful aims — winning at play, closing a bargain, finding a safe road — and were usually drawn on paper or wood and carried about the person. Because each of the ten signs answered a separate need, the family survives as a record of the everyday concerns that Icelandic folk magic was asked to serve.
source: Huld manuscript (Lbs 4626 8vo, 1860)

name: The Ljungby Horn
maker: Said to have belonged to a troll
powers: Drinking horn of the troll folk, kept in the church at Ljungby.
description: The Ljungby horn, a great drinking horn with gilded silver mounts that is kept at Trolle-Ljungby Castle in Scania (Skåne), southern Sweden. Legend says the trolls who live beneath the great boulder Maglestenen once feasted on golden pillars at Christmas, and that a stable hand who rode out on their feast night came away with their horn and their pipe. As he rode, the drink he was offered burnt his horse's flank like acid, and the trolls pursued him to the castle gate; when he reached the plowed field and rode a cross shape over it, the trolls could not follow. They cursed the castle — the horse and the rider died, and the castle burned three times — and the horn and pipe were kept within the walls forever after. The objects survive to this day and are shown to visitors as proof of the trolls' feast, making the horn one of the best-known relics of Swedish legend.
source: Småland legend of the Ljungby horn and pipe

name: The Ljungby Pipe
maker: Said to have belonged to a troll
powers: Blowing it was said to set people dancing against their will.
description: The Ljungby pipe, a whistle of carved bone or ivory kept together with the Ljungby horn at Trolle-Ljungby Castle in Scania, southern Sweden. In the legend the trolls beneath the boulder Maglestenen offered the pipe, together with their drinking horn, to a stable hand who came to their Christmas feast; it was playable from both ends and formed one half of the trolls' treasure. When the servant fled with the horn and the pipe, the trolls' pursuit broke against the cross-shaped furrows of the plowed field, and their curse fell on the castle instead. The pipe was long counted among the wonders of Trolle-Ljungby, kept beside the horn in a glass case that no one dared to open, for the trolls had warned that if the objects were ever removed the owner would meet great misfortune. Together the horn and pipe preserve the memory of a troll feast at a real Swedish castle.
source: Småland legend of the Ljungby horn and pipe

name: Lund Minster
maker: Romanesque cathedral; legend of the giant Finn
description: Lund Cathedral (Lund domkyrka), the great Romanesque church of the Swedish Middle Ages, begun in the late eleventh century when Lund was the seat of the archbishopric of the Nordic lands and consecrated in 1145. In legend the giant Finn built the cathedral in exchange for the sun and the moon, and was tricked out of his wages; in some versions he was turned to stone, and a carved giant figure still guards the crypt, stroking his beard while a column he was shaping bends above him. The crypt with its thick pillars and the twin towers over the high altar are among the finest Romanesque works in Scandinavia. The cathedral crowns the story 'Finn the Giant and the Minster of Lund', and the carved stone giant remains one of Lund's best-known sights.
source: Lund Cathedral; Scania legend of the giant Finn

name: The Luckstone
powers: Brings luck and wards off the mare and misfortune.
description: A luckstone (lyckosten), a stone with a natural hole, worn on a cord or kept in the pocket for luck and protection in Swedish folk tradition. Such pierced stones were also called 'hängesten', hanging stones, from the way they were strung and hung, and 'örngottsstenar'; they were hung in stables, on the neck, or by the bed to ward off the mare and misfortune, and the hole was the mark that gave the stone its power. In some districts the stone was hung over the stable door to keep the cattle safe, in others carried by sailors or travellers as a charm against storms and robbers. The lucky stone is known across the North Atlantic world as the 'witch stone' or 'hag stone', and the Swedish names record the same belief in the seeing and warding power of the pierced stone.
source: Swedish folk belief about pierced amulet stones

name: The Lapp Drum
powers: Used for divination and calling the spirit world.
description: The Lapp drum, the sacred drum of the Sami noaidi or shaman, made of a frame of pine with a reindeer-skin head painted with figures in alder-bark juice. The drum was beaten for divination, and the noaidi sought answers in the drumming while its figures of sun, gods, reindeer, and man mirrored the Sami cosmos; a pointer or ring moving across the painted skin gave the answer to the question asked. Many drums were confiscated by missionaries in the 17th-18th centuries and burned or sent to collections, so that only a few dozen survive in museums, each one an irreplaceable map of the old belief. The drum's power was believed to travel with its owner, and the noaidi used it to find lost reindeer, cure the sick, and travel between the worlds. The Lapp drum is the central object of the older Sami religion and a key witness to it.
source: Sami drum tradition; museum collections

name: Lavvu
material: Wood poles with reindeer-hide or canvas covering
description: The conical tent of the Sámi people, raised on a tripod of poles and covered with reindeer hide or, in modern times, canvas. The lavvu is light enough to carry on a sledge or a reindeer and quick to pitch on the open tundra, with the hearth at the center and smoke escaping through the crown. It has been the seasonal home of reindeer-herding families for centuries and is still raised at festivals. The layout of the lavvu follows a strict order, with the back of the tent and the space opposite the door kept sacred and reserved, and the family's places arranged around the fire by rank and custom. In winter the hide cover and the inner snow-wall turned the tent into a warm shelter against the Arctic cold, and in summer the lighter canvas version followed the herds. The lavvu remains the pattern for modern Sámi life, at once a practical tent and a symbol of the herding culture.
source: Sámi ethnography

name: The Lur
description: A long S-shaped horn of hammered bronze from the Nordic Bronze Age, cast with an ornamental disc at the mouth and decorated in fine raised bosses and engraving. More than fifty lurs survive, most from Denmark, found in peat bogs and hoards, including the famous Brudevaelte lurs from Zealand. Their curved form and fine workmanship make them among the oldest surviving brass instruments in the world, and they were likely sounded in cult and sacrifice, perhaps in pairs, as Bronze Age rock carvings suggest. The lur also gave its name to the later wooden folk horns of the region, though the two are quite different instruments.
source: Bronze Age bog finds, Denmark

name: Lituus of Romulus
powers: Marked the regions of the sky for augury at Rome's foundation; found unharmed after the burning of the Curia Saliorum.
description: The lituus of Romulus was the curved augur's staff with which, in Roman tradition, Rome's founder marked out the regions of the sky when he took the auspices that sanctioned the building of the city. The relic was kept among the sacred gear of the Salian priests in the Curia Saliorum on the Palatine, and Cicero, Plutarch, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus record how it was found unharmed after the building burned, a survival read as a portent that the augural science, and with it Rome's favour with the gods, would endure. The lituus, a crook-like staff, was the professional badge of the augur, used to trace the templum, the sacred area of the sky, before any public act, and its shape became the pattern of the augur's staff in all later Roman state ritual. The Romulus relic belongs with the ancile and the fire of Vesta among the talismanic objects on which Rome's continuance was thought to hang. No such staff survives; the legends are our only record of it.
source: Cicero, De Divinatione; Plutarch, Life of Camillus; Dionysius of Halicarnassus

name: Luzzu
era: Traditional working boat (modern form early 20th century)
maker: Maltese boatwrights, family yards at Marsaxlokk and Gozo
powers: The painted Eye of Osiris on the prow wards off the evil eye and guides the boat home.
description: The luzzu, the brightly painted wooden fishing boat of the Maltese islands, carries on its prow a pair of apotropaic eyes painted on either side of the bow, an inheritance many trace to the Eye of Osiris or of Horus of the ancient Mediterranean, meant to ward off the evil eye, protect the crew, and guide the boat home to a good catch. The boats, broad-beamed and high-prowed, are built and repaired by family yards at Marsaxlokk and on Gozo, painted in reds, blues, yellows, and greens, with the eyes and often a patron saint's image or a religious motto on the bows. Though the modern luzzu form dates only from the early 20th century, the eye motif is ancient and links the boats to a seafaring world older than Malta's recorded history. The working fleet of Marsaxlokk harbour, still bright with the painted gaze, is one of the most photographed sights of the island. The luzzu stands for the persistence of a Mediterranean folk belief on the decks of modern boats.
source: Ethnographic and maritime documentation of the Maltese fishing tradition

name: Lia Fáil
powers: Cried out beneath the rightful king of Ireland when he stood on it.
description: Lia Fáil, the Stone of Destiny, stands on the hill of Tara and is one of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann in Irish tradition. In the Lebor Gabála Érenn it is counted among the treasures carried into Ireland, and later tales say the stone cried out beneath the rightful king when he stood or stepped on it, so that the whole assembly heard its voice. The best-known account is in Baile in Scáil, where the stone roars under the high king Conn of the Hundred Battles and reveals the line of kings who will follow him. Medieval writers and antiquaries long claimed that the Irish stone was the same as the Stone of Scone used in the coronation of the kings of Scotland, a belief still attached to the Lia Fáil by visitors to Tara. The present standing stone on the hill is a weathered monolith, and its identification with the legendary stone is itself a matter of debate. It remains the most potent symbol of Irish kingship.
source: Lebor Gabála Érenn; Baile in Scáil

name: Lukasa Memory Board
description: The lukasa is a wooden memory board of the Luba peoples of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, its surface covered with beads, shells, and metal pins arranged in clusters that encode historical and ritual knowledge. A member of the Mbudye association, the court's body of historians, reads the board by touch, tracing the beads as a mnemonic that calls forth genealogies, royal protocol, migration legends, and the esoteric teachings of the kingdom. Because each board belonged to a particular specialist and was arranged to fit his memory, no two lukasa are identical, and the objects were kept secret from the uninitiated. The tradition is bound to the founding legends of the Luba state, and the boards are still referenced in the stories of the culture heroes Kalala Ilunga and Mbidi Kiluwe. Scholars such as Mary Nooter Roberts have studied the lukasa as a case of embodied, non-written memory, and the boards are among the best-known objects of Central African court art. Luba historians and diviners continue to use them in their work today.
source: Luba court tradition; scholarly studies (M. Nooter Roberts)

name: Lozi Royal Barge
description: The Lozi royal barge, the nalikwanda, is the great wooden vessel that carries the Litunga, the king of the Lozi people of western Zambia, at the Kuomboka ceremony. When the annual floods rise on the Zambezi, the king leaves the lowland palace and is paddled in procession to higher ground, the barge covered with an immense shroud of black-and-white cloth and surrounded by dozens of escort boats. The crossing is the climax of Kuomboka, a pageant that renews the bond between the king and the waters that shape Lozi life, and the barge's heavy, deliberate movement through the flood is timed to the songs of its rowers. The nalikwanda is built of timber by Lozi boatbuilders, and a new barge is commissioned when the old one fails. Kuomboka, whose name means 'to get out of the water', draws thousands of spectators each year. The barge is the central object of the most famous river festival in southern Africa.
source: Lozi Kuomboka tradition; ethnographic accounts

name: Lei Niho Palaoa (Whale-Tooth Pendant)
description: Pendant of the Hawaiian chiefs made from a carved sperm whale tooth suspended on a braid of human hair, worn by men and women of high rank. The hair cord was itself a gift of honour, braided from hair offered by relatives and friends of the wearer, and the whole ornament was kapu — forbidden to anyone beneath the chiefly class. The lei niho palaoa signalled genealogical status and royal favour, and after the arrival of whalers and traders whale teeth and later ivory from walrus tusks were carved in its place, so that the oldest examples, in the richest carving and finest hair-work, are the most treasured heirlooms of Hawaiian families.
material: sperm whale tooth, braided human hair
maker: Hawaiian craftsmen of the chiefly class
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Hawaiian adornment

name: Lietuviška Juosta
description: Hand-woven sash of linen and wool, rich with geometric patterns in several colours, worn by Lithuanian men and women wrapped at the waist over festive dress and given as gifts at weddings, christenings and funerals. The juosta was woven on narrow looms or by tablet weaving, and every region knew its own ornament — rhombuses, zigzags, crosses and small stars — so that a sash could name the wearer's parish. In folk belief the sash was protective: it binds, fastens and marks a sacred boundary, and a woven band given away could carry goodwill or serve as an offering, mediating between people and the spirits of field and forest.
source: Ethnographic studies of Lithuanian sash symbolism (Lietuvių juostų simbolika, Lituanistika)

name: Lielvārde Belt
description: The Lielvārde belt: a wide woven wool sash of red-and-white geometric patterns, with small figures worked into the bands, worn with Latvian folk costume and woven in the Lielvārde region of central Latvia. Folklore remembers it as a protective band that warded off evil, and since the 1970s the repeating patterns have been read by some as a hidden code of the universe — even of human DNA — a theory championed in popular writing though not by all scholars. The folklorist Janīna Kursīte traces its red-white symbolism to ancient protective clothing and incantations, and the belt was admitted to the Latvian Cultural Canon in 2008 as a national symbol.
maker: Latvian village weavers of the Lielvārde region
source: Latvijas Kultūras kanons: Lielvārdas josta (2008); folklore researcher Janīna Kursīte

name: Laima's Distaff
description: The distaff of fate in Latvian and Lithuanian belief: a carved spindle-holder on which the goddess Laima, or the forest fairy Lauma, spins and measures the thread of a human life, fixing its length and its luck. Folk accounts describe laumas borrowing distaffs and spindles from village women and spinning linen by night, and the spindle's turning thread stands in countless spinning dainas for fate being spun out for a newborn child. The distaff itself was a treasured, often carved and painted object passed from mother to daughter, so that the homely tool of flax-spinning carried a double meaning: the thread of cloth and the thread of destiny.
source: Latvian and Lithuanian folklore accounts of Laima and laumas as spinners of fate (Latvian dainas; Britannica: Laima)

name: Lajkonik
description: The Lajkonik is the hobby-horse rider of Kraków, a bearded figure in pointed Tatar dress and Mongol robes who parades the Old Town each year on the first Thursday after Corpus Christi, playfully striking onlookers with his gilded wooden mace to bring them good luck. Legend traces the custom to 1287, when Vistula raftsmen of the Zwierzyniec district, called włóczkowie, are said to have surprised and overwhelmed a sleeping Tatar raiding party camped by the river, then ridden into the city dressed in the captives' robes to celebrate their victory. The earliest written notices of the procession date from the 1730s and 1750s, and the mayor still greets the Lajkonik at the Main Market Square with a ceremonial ransom of money and a toast drunk from a chalice. The key elements of its costume, from the cream-crested head to the golden mace, were designed in 1909 by Stanisław Wyspiański, and the figure remains one of the unofficial symbols of Kraków, reproduced on trams, shop signs and festival posters.
source: Ethnographic studies of Kraków folk festivals

name: Lahij Copperware
description: Lahij copperware is the hammered copper and brass craft of the mountain village of Lahij in Azerbaijan's Ismayilli district, where smiths have worked for centuries in a tight warren of craftsmen's streets. A vessel such as an ewer, basin, cauldron or tray is raised from a single sheet of metal by hammering, never cast or soldered, then engraved with geometric rosettes, floral scrolls and inscriptions, and finally coated with a silvery tin alloy that protects the copper. The craft flourished in the nineteenth century, when Lahij's copper goods travelled the Silk Road and were sold in Baku, Tbilisi and Persian cities, and the village's self-governing craft guilds kept the techniques alive. In 2015 UNESCO inscribed the copper craftsmanship of Lahij on the Representative List, and master coppersmiths still work in the old street, training apprentices in hammer, chisel and furnace.
source: UNESCO ICH 'Copper craftsmanship of Lahij' (2015)

name: Latvian Josta (Woven Belt)
description: Ornamental belt woven by Latvian women on a small rigid loom, patterned with geometric symbols of the sun, moon and stars and the zigzag josta motif, worn by men to hold shirt and breeches. A full-length josta measures several metres and is wound twice around the waist; its weaving is a living craft, and the Latvian National Centre for Culture keeps a register of master weavers. The belt is part of the national costume worn at song festivals, and its symbols are read as protective signs: the sun for light, the grass snake for the household, and the endless repeating band for continuity. Traditionally the josta was a woman's gift, woven for her husband or son, and a richly patterned belt showed both the weaver's skill and the family's standing. Museum examples from the 19th century show the standard red, white and green palette with the black zigzag that gives the belt its name.
source: Latvian National Centre for Culture (josta pattern register)
